note: Narration templates for the guided tours. Figures come from {placeholders} filled from the live data; conclusions are chosen by rules in the app ({"by": fact, "cases": {...}}). The weekly tour agent may refine wording and choose examples, within the rules checked by tools/validate.py.

gap.title: Is AI shrinking the gap from research to change?

intro.say: Each arc is one research breakthrough, coloured by where it began: a university, a government lab or industry. It runs from the start of research to the first product. Where mainstream use followed, a thinner arc continues to that date.

yes: For example: {exTitle}. Research {exWhere} began in {exR}; the first product came in {exP}
cases.no: Select any arc to see its story.

say: Here is a century of breakthroughs

cases.yes: . Where mainstream use has followed, it typically came {adopt} years after the first product.

cases.shrunk: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has shrunk: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, {recent} for research since 2000.
cases.grown: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has grown: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, {recent} for research since 2000.
cases.flat: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has barely changed: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, {recent} for research since 2000.
cases.unclear: There is not yet enough data to say how the gap from research to first product has changed overall.

say: But much recent research has not yet reached a first product. Counting that unfinished work,

cases.holds: the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about {kmYears} years, still clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
cases.weakens: the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about {kmYears} years, so it is not clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
cases.tooEarly: it is too early to be sure.
cases.unclear: there is not yet enough data to tell.

gapchart.say: The gap-over-time chart follows this decade by decade, then adds scenarios beyond today, including AI and digital twins.

cases.ai: Since 2000, AI itself has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product, at about {fastestYears} years.
cases.other: Since 2000, {fastestName} has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product; AI ranks {aiRankWord} of {nFields} fields.

say: Select one field, as here with AI, and its sub-fields get their own tracks.

cases.faster: Since 2010, AI-driven work has been quicker: {ai} years, against {oth} for the rest.
cases.slower: Since 2010, AI-driven work has taken longer: {ai} years, against {oth} for the rest.
cases.similar: Since 2010, AI-driven work has taken about as long as the rest: {ai} years against {oth}.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.

cases.faster: Ahead, AI-assisted work is expected to be quicker: {aiOut} years, against {convOut} for conventional work.
cases.slower: Ahead, the estimates suggest AI-assisted work will take longer than conventional work.
cases.similar: Ahead, the estimates show little difference.

say: So, is AI shrinking the gap?

cases.0: None of the four measures here points to yes.
cases.1: One of the four measures here points to yes.
cases.2: Two of the four measures here, half, point to yes.
cases.3: Three of the four measures here point to yes.
cases.4: All four measures here point to yes.

say: The answer updates as new evidence arrives.

heatchart.say: The heatmap shows how the typical gap varies by field and by decade. Since 2010, {fastField} has been quickest and {slowField} slowest.

aichart.say: Each dot is one milestone, and the teal dots are AI-driven. For research since 2010, those typically took about {aiMed} years to reach a first product, against {restMed} for the rest.

horizon.title: What AI-assisted products are on the horizon for the energy system?

intro.say: The government's AI for clean energy vision is split into distinct areas. Diamonds mark stories linked to it, playing through from 1980 onwards.

radar.say: The Vision radar shows how close the technologies in each area are to everyday use: {nResearch} still in research, {nPilot} in pilots, {nCommercial} in early commercial use and {nScale} widely used. Of these, {nGB} are already used in Great Britain.

cases.some: The search agents have added {newCount} items in the last three months, including {newTitle}. Mark them as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.
cases.none: Nothing new has arrived in the last three months. Mark the radar as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.

cases.some: Looking five years ahead, {nextCount} products are expected. The soonest is {nextTitle}, around {nextYear}, and {busiestArea} has the most on the way.
cases.none: In the current data, no products are expected to arrive within the next five years.

changes.say: The Forecast drift chart shows when each clean energy technology is expected to arrive, and how those dates have moved as the agents re-estimate them.

slide.say: For a briefing, the PowerPoint report window creates a single-slide summary covering every area of the vision, ready to drop into a deck.

say: So, what is on the horizon?

cases.busy: A busy pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are closest to everyday use.
cases.steady: A steady pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are moving towards everyday use.
cases.quiet: Little has appeared in the data so far, so keep an eye on the radar as the agents search each week.

pipechart.say: The pipeline chart follows each technology from its area, through its readiness, to whether Great Britain has deployed it. So far, {pipeGB} of {pipeTotal} have been deployed there.

intro.say: New technology can give attackers new ways in. The filter on screen picks out the {attackPct} per cent of technologies here that widen this 'attack surface', from smart devices at the edge of the grid to AI agents.

say: The Cyber lens shows how long security took to catch up:

cases.slow: typically {lag} years after a technology arrived, a long time to leave systems exposed.
cases.moderate: typically {lag} years after a technology arrived.
cases.fast: typically within {lag} years of a technology arriving.
cases.unclear: the data does not yet show this clearly.

cases.some: Gaps remain. Since 2010, some technologies have arrived with no security response yet recorded in their category. They are shown first. So far that applies to {gapCount}, including {gapTitle}.
cases.none: In this data, every technology that has arrived since 2010 has a security response recorded in its category.

example.say: Each story card names a risk and suggests ways to reduce it, mapped to recognised guidance: the National Cyber Security Centre's Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), Ofgem's CAF Overlay, NIST, NERC CIP and IEC 62443.

cases.some: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications. The latest: {guideTitle}.
cases.none: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications.

caution.say: This is AI research to prompt discussion, not security advice. Always engage qualified experts, and your regulator where relevant.

cases.improving: Security is catching up faster than it used to.
cases.worsening: Security is taking longer to catch up than it used to.
cases.flat: The pace of catching up has barely changed.

secchart.say: This chart shows how many years each technology waited before a security response was recorded. Of those that have one, the longest wait was for {secLongestTitle}, at {secLongestYears} years.

intro.say: Research does not just change products; it can also make fortunes. This chart, Time to a fortune, follows founders from starting a company to the stock market listing, sale or valuation that made them rich.

research.say: Of {nFortunes} fortunes here, {nResearch} began in a university or research lab. So research is not only a route to new products: for some founders, it is where the money began.

cases.faster: The journey from founding to fortune is getting shorter: about {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015.
cases.slower: The journey from founding to fortune is getting longer: about {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015.
cases.similar: The journey from founding to fortune is about as long as ever: roughly {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough fortunes from recently founded companies to compare eras.

fastest.say: Sorted by speed, the quickest journey so far comes first: {fastestCo}, which took {fastestTime} to go from founding to fortune.

cases.faster: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK reached a product in {ukYears} years, faster than the {rowYears} years in the rest of the world.
cases.slower: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK took {ukYears} years to reach a product, slower than the {rowYears} years in the rest of the world.
cases.similar: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK reached a product in about the same time as in the rest of the world: {ukYears} years against {rowYears}.
cases.unclear: With the filter set to the UK only, there is not yet enough evidence to say whether UK research reaches a product faster or slower than research elsewhere.

uni.say: Now the filter shows university projects: {nUni} of them are still under way. They could become the next breakthroughs, and perhaps the next fortunes.

table.say: The Table lists every milestone. Sort by any column, such as the gap between milestones, and select a row to read its story.

cases.similar: the journey takes about as long as ever.
cases.unclear: it is too early to say whether the journey is getting faster or slower.

fortchart.say: Play the race through time. Each bubble is a fortune, sized by net worth. Gold rings mark the {fortResearch} of {fortCount} founders whose companies grew out of research.

intro.say: This model is maintained by AI agents that run every week. It holds {nMilestones} milestones so far.

research.say: A research agent searches for new breakthroughs and products across every field of AI, including each area of AI for clean energy. Everything it adds appears in the 'Data changes' view.

qa.say: A second agent checks each new entry independently. It requires more than one source, and the quoted evidence must really appear on the cited page. Nothing is ever deleted.

more.say: Further agents track new security guidance, shown here in the Cyber lens, and keep these walk-throughs up to date. Every change must pass automatic checks before it is published.

say: The 'Data quality' view shows that {pctSourceCited} percent of records now cite a checked source.

cases.scored: Once a forecast's outcome is known, it is scored against what actually happened. Forecasts scored so far: {fcResolved}.
cases.none: Each forecast is recorded now and will be scored against what actually happens once the outcome is known.

labels.say: Every record is labelled to show how it was produced and checked: source-cited, AI-compiled or AI estimate. You can filter records by these labels.

arrange.say: Choose an arrangement to lay out the windows for exploring, presenting, analysing or an AI for clean energy briefing. You can save any view or share it as a link.

answer.say: Help and the 'i' information buttons explain each feature. This model is maintained by AI, so it may contain errors. Check anything important against the original sources.

whatifchart.say: The What if? chart estimates how much sooner projected technologies could arrive if practical AI levers, such as faster discovery, simulation and approvals, were applied. An agent researches these levers every week.

say: Across {nGap} landed milestones, the longest journey was {longestTitle}, at {longestYears} years. Among recent arrivals, {quickRecentTitle} took just {quickRecentYears}.
Since 2010, {fastField} has been quickest, at about {fastFieldYears} years, and {slowField} slowest, at about {slowFieldYears}.

cases.yes: {improvedField} improved most: from {improvedFrom} years in the 1990s to {improvedTo} in the 2010s.
cases.no: No field has clearly sped up between the 1990s and the 2010s.

cases.faster: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work took about {aiMed} years to reach a product, against {restMed} for everything else. The AI-driven group is still small: {aiCount} milestones.
cases.similar: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has taken about as long to reach a product as the rest: {aiMed} years against {restMed}.
cases.slower: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has taken longer to reach a product: {aiMed} years against {restMed}.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.

say: Of {pipeTotal} clean energy technologies, {pipeResearch} are in research, {pipePilot} piloting, {pipeCommercial} in first commercial use and {pipeScale} at scale; {pipeGB} are deployed in Great Britain.

cases.early: Most are still early, so proving them at scale is the next challenge.
cases.late: Most have reached commercial use, so scaling up is the challenge now.

say: {driftCount} forecasts are being tracked; {driftPeakYear} is the busiest year, with {driftPeakCount} expected to arrive.

cases.none: None has been revised yet. Trails will appear here if the weekly re-estimates push any forecast back.
cases.some: {driftRevised} have been revised so far, and {driftSlipped} of those are now expected later than first forecast.

say: Security protections have typically arrived about {secMedian} years after the technology they protect. The longest wait here was for {secLongestTitle}, at {secLongestYears} years.

cases.open: {secOpen} still have no security response in their category.
cases.closed: Every technology here now has a security response in its category.

say: Of {fortCount} fortunes tracked here, {fortResearch} began in a university or research lab. The quickest to be made was {fortFastest}, in {fortFastestTime}.

cases.faster: Recent fortunes have been made faster than earlier ones.
cases.slower: Recent fortunes have taken longer to make than earlier ones.
cases.similar: Recent fortunes have taken about as long to make as earlier ones.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough recent fortunes to compare them with earlier ones.

whatif.say: In this scenario, practical AI levers bring projected technologies forward by about {wiAvg} years on average. By 2030, {wi2030AI} would arrive, against {wi2030Now} on current trends. The biggest lever is {wiTopLever}. It is an illustration, not a forecast.

cases.some: The agents added {newCount} milestones this week, including {newTitles}.
cases.none: No new milestones were added this week, so this is a review of the evidence.

w1.say: Across {nGap} milestones that have reached real use, the longest journey from lab to first use was {longestTitle}, at {longestYears} years. The quickest recent arrival, {quickRecentTitle}, made it in {quickRecentYears}.

w2.say: For AI for clean energy, {pipeTotal} technologies are tracked. {pipeResearch} are still at the research stage and only {pipeScale} have reached scale, so most of the vision is still ahead of us.

w3.say: The what-if scenario asks how much AI could speed things up. On today's pace, {wi2030Now} arrive by 2030; with the AI levers, {wi2030AI}. The biggest lever is {wiTopLever}. This is a scenario, not a forecast.

w4.say: Forecasts move. Of {driftCount} predictions tracked, {driftRevised} have been revised and {driftSlipped} have slipped. Expected dates are best treated as moving targets.

w5.say: Security still trails new technology by about {secMedian} years, and {secOpen} gaps remain open. The longest lag is {secLongestTitle}, at {secLongestYears} years.

open.say: This is the Gap explorer. Use the tabs at the top to switch between charts. Your filters apply to every chart. Selecting a milestone opens its story and also moves the What if? model to that point.

gapsort.say: In the Gap explorer you can sort and colour the bars. Drag across the chart to zoom into years; double-click to reset.

filter.say: The filter bar narrows any chart by search, field or origin. With fewer items, the rows grow larger and the years zoom in automatically.

heat.say: In the heatmap, select a cell to list its milestones in the side panel. The panel stays while you open a story.

ai.say: In AI against the rest, drag a box to zoom in; labels appear once there is room. Switch to select mode to list a group of milestones.

pipe.say: The pipeline follows technologies through their stages of development. Select any bar or flow to list the technologies behind it.

drift.say: In Forecast drift, the bars count expected arrivals by year. Select a bar to list them; trails show any slips as forecasts are revised.

sec.say: Security lag can be sorted by arrival, longest wait, or open gaps first. Rows in red still have no security response.

fort.say: Press play to watch the race to a fortune unfold over time, or select a bubble to read that company's story.

whatif.say: What if? applies practical AI levers. Switch the scenario or the levers, and select a row to see the reasoning and any research behind it.

insight.say: Finally, the Insight button gives this week's analysis of each chart, with subtitles and speech. Select any number to see what lies behind it. You can also save any chart as an image or CSV.

say: AI for clean energy: this week's analysis, updated {cleanUpdatedAt}.

cases.some: The agents added {cleanNewCount} clean energy technologies this week, including {cleanNewTitles}.
cases.none: No clean energy technologies were added this week, so this is a review of the pipeline.

c1.say: Does AI speed things up? Since 2010, the {aiCount} AI-driven milestones took a median of {aiMed} years to land, against {restMed} for the rest. The group is small and the evidence is mixed, so treat this as a hint, not proof.

c2.say: Journeys vary hugely. {longestTitle} took {longestYears} years, while {quickRecentTitle} arrived in {quickRecentYears}. No researched stories are ready to retell this week, so pick any arc to follow a technology from lab to first use.

c3.say: One shift on the AI for clean energy radar: AI assurance for energy, the work of checking that AI tools can be trusted on the grid, moved from research to pilot.

c4.say: Security has typically trailed deployment by about {secMedian} years. The longest wait was {secLongestTitle}, at {secLongestYears} years. Guidance updates were logged this week, but that gap is still where the risk sits.

c5.say: Can we trust forecasts? We track {driftCount} of them. Expectations were revised {driftRevised} times and {driftSlipped} slipped. That is a reminder that arrival dates for clean energy technologies are best read as estimates.

c6.say: What if AI levers were pulled harder? In this scenario, {wiTopLever} matters most, moving the outcome from {wi2030Now} to {wi2030AI}. It is a model, not a forecast, and levers are researched for only some technologies.
